newsitem.title: CANADA: FOCUS-Thomson profits fall in transition year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thomson profits fall in transition year.

text.p: Global publishing and travel company Thomson Corp., in the throes of digesting last year's $3.4 billion acquisition of West Publishing Co., suffered a drop in core earnings in 1996.
Net earnings after extraordinaries for the year were $569 million, or $0.95 per share. This is compared with $789 million and $1.34 a share.
Excluding gains on asset sales, earnings were $412 million and earnings per common share were $0.69, compared with $439 million and $0.74. Revenues were $7.72 billion in 1996 as versus $7.23 billion.

Results for 1996 included a dilution of $0.05 a share for West and a dilution of $0.08 per share from disposals in 1995 and 1996. Earnings for 1996 included $156 million in gains on disposals of businesses while in 1995 they included $350 million in gains on disposal of businesses, net of tax.
Thomson said the lower level of pre-extraordinary earnings was due to the loss of earnings from asset sales along with the hit taken because of acquisitions, primarily West.
"When you sell assets and you do acquisitions, you can't do that overnight," said CrediFinance Securities analyst Benoit Dube.
"It takes time to integrate and it takes time to get back to the level of profit you had before. So 1996 for Thomson is a year of transition," he added.
In the past decade, Thomson has bought more than 350 businesses and sold about 200.
Its major holdings now include West, The Globe and Mail newspaper, Britain's second-largest charter airline and the Lunn Poly chain of travel agencies.
"This major repositioning is now largely behind us, and the benefits in terms of shareholder value are becoming increasingly apparent," Thomson said.
Dube said he thinks that in the mid to long-term, Thomson is on the right track.
Thomson shares dropped 0.35 to 29.85 on the Toronto Stock Exchange.
